about: The US Mint's silver bullion coin and the most traded one in the country. Each holds one troy ounce of .999 silver, with the weight and purity backed by the US government. The design changed partway through 2021 from the heraldic eagle to an eagle landing, so you'll find both versions dated that year.

faq.q: What is a 1 oz Silver Eagle worth today?
faq.a: Its melt value is one troy ounce of silver at spot, because every Silver Eagle holds exactly one troy ounce of .999 fine silver. The live figure on this page updates through the trading day. What a dealer charges or pays will sit above or below that, since melt is only the metal.

faq.q: Why do Silver Eagles cost more than spot?
faq.a: The price over spot is the premium. It covers the US Mint's own charge to its dealers, shipping, insurance and each dealer's margin. Silver Eagles usually carry a bigger premium than bars or other one ounce coins because demand for them is steady and the Mint sells them only through authorized buyers.

faq.q: Is a Silver Eagle worth more than its one dollar face value?
faq.a: Yes, by a wide margin. The one dollar face makes it legal tender, but nobody spends one at face, because the silver inside is worth many times that. Treat the face value as a formality and value the coin by its silver content at spot.

faq.q: Do the 2021 Type 2 Silver Eagles hold the same silver?
faq.a: Yes. The design changed partway through 2021 from the heraldic eagle to an eagle landing, and the Mint added security features, but both types hold one troy ounce of .999 fine silver. Their melt value is identical. Some 2021 Type 1 and Type 2 versions draw collector interest, which is separate from melt.

faq.q: What will a dealer pay me for a Silver Eagle?
faq.a: Most dealers buy common date Silver Eagles back at or a little above melt, depending on demand that week. The quickest way to know is to ask two or three dealers for their buy price on the same day and compare it with the live melt value on this page.

faq.q: Are proof or graded Silver Eagles worth more than melt?
faq.a: Often, yes. Proof coins, low mintage years and coins graded by PCGS or NGC sell on collector demand as well as silver, so melt is the floor rather than the price. Check a price guide or ask a dealer for anything that isn't a plain bullion coin.

faq.q: How much is a tube of 20 Silver Eagles worth?
faq.a: A mint tube holds 20 coins, so its melt value is 20 troy ounces of silver at spot. Pick 20 in the quick amounts on this page to see the live total. A sealed monster box from the Mint holds 500 coins, or 25 tubes.

faq.a: Each Silver Maple Leaf holds one troy ounce of .9999 fine silver, so its melt value is the silver spot price. The live figure is shown on this page. Dealers sell it above melt and usually buy it back near melt.

faq.q: Does a Maple Leaf hold more silver than a Silver Eagle?
faq.a: Both are one troy ounce bullion coins, and dealers and this page value each at one ounce of silver. The Maple Leaf is .9999 fine and the Silver Eagle is .999 fine, a difference of a tenth of a percent that no dealer prices in. What separates them in practice is the premium.

faq.q: Why are Maple Leaf premiums often lower?
faq.a: The Royal Canadian Mint strikes Maple Leafs in large numbers and sells them widely, so dealers often price them closer to spot than Silver Eagles. That isn't fixed. Premiums move with demand, so compare the price over spot from a few dealers on the same day.

faq.q: What are the radial lines and the small privy mark?
faq.a: Since 2014 the Royal Canadian Mint has struck fine radial lines into the background and a tiny maple leaf mark with the year's last two digits. Both are anti counterfeiting features. Recent coins also carry the Mint's Bullion DNA, which lets authorized dealers verify a coin.

faq.q: How much silver is in a Morgan dollar?
faq.a: A Morgan dollar weighs 26.73 grams and is 90% silver and 10% copper, so it holds 0.77344 troy oz of pure silver. That figure comes from the coin's legal weight and fineness, and it's the number every melt calculation for a Morgan starts from.

faq.q: What is a Morgan dollar worth in melt?
faq.a: Its melt value is 0.77344 troy oz times silver spot. The live figure on this page moves with the silver price. Melt is the floor for a Morgan, since even worn common dates usually sell for a little more than their metal.

faq.q: When is a Morgan worth more than melt?
faq.a: Key dates, scarce mint marks like Carson City, and coins in high grades can be worth far more than their silver. The date and the small letter on the back under the wreath matter most. Check a price guide or show the coin to a dealer before you sell it for melt.

faq.q: Are the new US Mint Morgan dollars the same silver?
faq.a: No. The Morgans the US Mint has struck since 2021 are .999 fine silver, not the 90% silver of the originals, and they sell as collector coins. This page covers the original Morgans struck from 1878 to 1904 and in 1921.

faq.q: What are full bands on a Mercury dime?
faq.a: Full bands describes a coin whose horizontal bands on the reverse fasces are fully split and rounded. It marks a strong strike and sharp detail, and grading services note it. Full band coins can sell for far more than ordinary ones of the same date, well above melt.

faq.q: Do all Mercury dimes hold the same silver?
faq.a: Yes. Every Mercury dime from 1916 to 1945 weighs 2.5 grams and is 90% silver, so each one holds the same 0.0723 troy oz. Wear can shave off a little metal, which is why dealers sometimes quote worn coins slightly under full melt.

faq.a: No. The US switched dimes to a copper and nickel clad coin in 1965, so a circulated 1965 dime holds no silver at all. The easy check is the edge. A silver dime shows a solid silver color, while a clad dime shows a copper stripe.

faq.q: Are any silver dimes worth more than melt?
faq.a: Some are. Key dates, rare mint marks and coins in high grades sell to collectors for more than their silver. Most worn Roosevelt dimes trade near melt, so look up the date and mint mark in a price guide or ask a coin dealer before you sell a whole roll.

faq.q: What is a 1 oz Gold Eagle worth?
faq.a: Its melt value is one troy ounce of gold at spot, because each one ounce Gold Eagle holds exactly one troy ounce of pure gold. The live figure is shown on this page. Dealers sell above that figure and usually buy back near it.

faq.q: If it's 22 karat, is it really 1 oz of gold?
faq.a: Yes. The coin is 91.67% gold with a little silver and copper added to make it harder, so it weighs 33.931 grams in all. The extra weight is the alloy. The pure gold inside is still exactly one troy ounce, as the US Mint states.

faq.q: Should I compare a Gold Eagle with a Gold Buffalo?
faq.a: Both hold one troy ounce of gold and have the same melt value. The Buffalo is 24 karat .9999 gold and a little softer, while the Eagle's 22 karat alloy resists scratches. Premiums differ by dealer and by week, so compare the price over spot rather than the coin.

faq.q: What premium over spot is normal for a Gold Eagle?
faq.a: Gold Eagles usually cost more over spot than gold bars or some foreign one ounce coins, because of the Mint's own markup and steady demand. The premium changes with the market, so compare a few dealers on the same day and look at the price over the live melt value here.

faq.q: What will a dealer pay for a Gold Eagle?
faq.a: Dealers usually buy common Gold Eagles back near melt, sometimes a little above it when demand is strong. Ask two or three dealers for their buy price on the same day and compare each one with the live melt value shown on this page.

faq.a: It holds 0.1 troy oz of pure gold, so its melt value is one tenth of the gold spot price. The live figure is shown on this page. Dealers charge more than that for the coin, and the gap is larger than it is on a one ounce coin.

faq.q: Why is the premium per ounce higher on small coins?
faq.a: Striking, packaging and handling cost about the same per coin whatever its size, so a tenth ounce coin carries those costs on far less gold. That pushes its price over spot up per ounce. Ten tenth ounce coins usually cost noticeably more than one full ounce coin.

faq.q: Do all 1/10 oz gold coins have the same melt value?
faq.a: Yes, if each one holds a tenth of a troy ounce of pure gold. A tenth ounce Gold Eagle, Gold Maple Leaf or Krugerrand all melt to the same figure, whatever their purity or total weight. Only the premium and how easily dealers take them back differ.

faq.q: Does the five dollar face value mean anything?
faq.a: Only that the coin is US legal tender. The gold inside is worth many times its face value, so nobody spends one at face. Value it by its gold content at spot, as this page does, and expect dealers to price it the same way.

faq.q: How does a Gold Buffalo compare with a Gold Eagle?
faq.a: Both hold exactly one troy ounce of gold and have the same melt value. The Buffalo is 24 karat .9999 gold and the Eagle is a harder 22 karat alloy. The Buffalo was the US Mint's first 24 karat gold coin, struck from 2006.

faq.q: Why does the Gold Buffalo weigh 31.108 grams?
faq.a: Pure gold at one troy ounce is 31.1035 grams. The Buffalo is .9999 fine rather than perfectly pure, so the Mint makes it a hair heavier to make sure each coin holds a full troy ounce of gold. That's the figure its melt value uses.

faq.q: What is a Krugerrand worth today?
faq.a: A one ounce Krugerrand holds exactly one troy ounce of pure gold, so its melt value is the gold spot price. The live figure is shown on this page. Krugerrands often carry one of the smaller premiums among gold coins because so many have been struck since 1967.

faq.q: Why is a Krugerrand heavier than one ounce?
faq.a: It's 22 karat, 91.67% gold with copper added for hardness, so the whole coin weighs 33.93 grams. The extra weight is the copper. The pure gold inside is 31.10 grams, which is exactly one troy ounce, and that's the part that sets its melt value.

faq.q: Does a Krugerrand have a face value?
faq.a: No. It's legal tender in South Africa, but it carries no face value in rand. It was designed to be valued by its gold content alone, and dealers price it that way, at the gold spot price plus a premium.

faq.q: How do I check a Krugerrand isn't fake?
faq.a: Start with weight and size. A real one ounce Krugerrand weighs 33.93 grams and measures about 32.77 mm across. A precise scale and calipers catch most fakes. A dealer can run a magnet test, a ping test or an XRF scan if you need more certainty.

faq.q: What sizes of Krugerrand exist?
faq.a: Besides the one ounce coin, Krugerrands have been struck since 1980 in half ounce, quarter ounce and tenth ounce sizes. Each holds that fraction of a troy ounce of pure gold, so its melt value is that fraction of the gold spot price.

faq.a: A one ounce Gold Maple Leaf holds one troy ounce of .9999 fine gold, so its melt value is the gold spot price. The live figure is shown on this page. Dealers sell above melt and usually buy back close to it.

faq.q: How is .9999 gold different from 22 karat?
faq.a: A .9999 coin is almost pure gold, while a 22 karat coin like the Gold Eagle or Krugerrand mixes in some copper or silver for hardness. Both one ounce coins hold exactly one troy ounce of gold, so their melt values match. Only the total weight differs.

faq.q: Is the Gold Maple Leaf easy to scratch?
faq.a: Pure gold is soft, so a Gold Maple Leaf marks more easily than a 22 karat coin. Handle it by the edge and keep it in its capsule. Small marks don't change its melt value, though dealers may pay a little less for a coin that looks rough.

faq.q: Does a Gold Maple Leaf cost less over spot than a Gold Eagle?
faq.a: Often, but not always. Gold Maple Leafs are widely traded and frequently priced a little closer to spot than Gold Eagles. Premiums change week to week, so compare the price over spot from a few dealers on the same day.
